title: Guilfoil Village (15Fa176), Fayette County
summary: Guilfoil Village (15Fa176) in Fayette County was a Middle Fort Ancient farming village of about AD 1000–1499. It is a protected site.
bodyMarkdown:
Guilfoil Village is a Middle [Fort Ancient](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fort_Ancient) farming village in Fayette County, recorded by archaeologists as site 15Fa176. It was listed on the [National Register of Historic Places](https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/NRIS/85003063) in 1985 under criterion of information potential. The Register’s period of significance is AD 1000 to 1499—the centuries when people lived there, not the year of the listing or any modern dig. This story uses those occupation years.

Fort Ancient is an archaeologists’ name for a shared way of life in the middle Ohio Valley from about 1000 to 1750 CE, not the name of a single tribe. The culture is known from southern Ohio, northern Kentucky, southeastern Indiana, and western West Virginia. Communities like Guilfoil farmed corn, beans, and squash—the “three sisters”—hunted deer and turkey, fished, and gathered nuts and mussels. Isotope studies at related sites suggest maize could supply roughly half or more of calories. People lived in semi-permanent villages of circular or rectangular houses, often arranged around an open plaza and sometimes ringed by a wooden stockade. Pottery was commonly shell-tempered and cordmarked. Triangular stone points, bone awls, and shell ornaments turn up in their sites. Trade brought marine shell from the Gulf Coast and copper from the Great Lakes.

Guilfoil belongs to the centuries just before sustained European contact, when farming villages like it were spread across central Kentucky and the wider middle Ohio Valley. It is a separate site from the other Fort Ancient villages already on the Kentucky History Drive map. The culture takes its name from the Fort Ancient Earthworks in Warren County, Ohio—a much earlier Hopewell ceremonial enclosure (about 100 BCE–400 CE) that nineteenth-century writers wrongly linked to these later villagers. The earthworks and the Fort Ancient culture are not the same thing.

What happened to Fort Ancient communities after about 1650 is still debated. Climate stress in the Little Ice Age, intergroup conflict, and European-introduced disease all figure in the explanations. Some archaeologists see possible links to historic Algonquian-speaking peoples of the Ohio Valley, including the Shawnee; direct lineages remain uncertain. Guilfoil itself is known from survey and limited investigation as a Middle Fort Ancient village of information potential—valuable for what its deposits can still teach, not as a reconstructed tourist site.

This is a protected archaeological site on private land. The address is restricted in the National Register record. Digging or collecting at archaeological sites without permission is a crime in Kentucky. Ask before you visit any site on private land.

## Kentucky today

This site names Guilfoil Village but does not map it to a street address; the pin is a rounded, county-level point in Fayette County only. Nearby towns are not used as locators in the body. Other Fort Ancient stories on this drive cover related villages without collapsing them into one. The Register listing and the occupation span of AD 1000–1499 are the public facts that matter here.
Source: [NPGallery / NRHP: Guilfoil Village Site (15FA176)](https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/NRIS/85003063)
